Context of the data: Vorwort p.III "im täglichen Verkehr mit den freundlichen Eingeborenen ihre Sprache zu erlernen und einen kleinen Theil ihrer Märchen, Sagen und Räthsel in wörtlicher Niederschrift aufzuzeichnen"; §1 pp.2-3 (verified on p.3 image) "... und meine Aufmerksamkeit weniger auf zarte Aussprachenuancen gerichtet, die zu ihrer Auffassung eine lange Gewöhnung des Ohres erfordern." and "Soweit die feinere Aussprache mit Bestimmtheit festgestellt war, habe ich sie im Lexikon vollständig angegeben, in den Texten dagegen sparsamer, nur so weit, als zur Vermeidung von groben Lesefehlern nötig schien."
morph.stmt: Morris §3 pp.7-8: "Ein Theil der Wörter kann Formativelemente (Prä-, In- und Suffixe) annehmen... Die Formativelemente sind: A. Präfixe 1) a 2) i 3) pu (mu) 4) pa (ma) 5) ma 6) tu 7) ta 8) ri 9) ra. B. Suffixe 1) i 2) an. C. Infixe 1) in." — i.e. the derivational/voice/aspect inventory is predominantly prefixal (nine prefixes vs. two suffixes and one rare infix), supplemented by suffixal nominalisers (-at/-kät etc., p.14), the genitive linker -n/-t, and enclitic person/possessor words (-ku, -nu/-m, -inja/'nja, -mäi, -ta, -mui, -ra; §13 p.33) that count for stress; "Der Vokal sämmtlicher Präfixe kann vor vokalisch anlautenden Nomina elidirt werden" (p.12).

228.cfw: Morris 1900, Adriani 1928 and Lenggang, Nio, Zainil and Adam 1978 all place Mentawai main stress on the penultimate syllable (with a closed set of final-stressed words and an echo-vowel final syllable that does not count), but Arifin, Malano and Kasim 1992, a phonology monograph on the same Sikakap dialect, state in one paragraph without examples that stress falls on the final syllable, so the penultimate reading is well supported but not uncontested.

corr.head: Source denies intensity-based word stress; only a slight, hedged penult lengthening
corr.detail: StressTyp2 codes a word-level penultimate pattern (10 010 0010 00010 000010 0000010 00000010), but the cited source says that syllable stress of the Dutch (intensity) type 'does not exist in Minangkabau' (equal force on every syllable of a word) and grants only that the penultimate syllable 'sounds somewhat longer... and has, one might to that extent say, the main tone', clearly so only when the penult is open, and with speakers disagreeing on placement (kaLAkuan ~ kalaKUan). Sentence stress (woordtoon) is treated separately (p. XV). The language is listed as a dominant pattern, not as an exceptionless one.

229.prule: No intensity difference among the syllables of a word (equal force on every syllable); the penultimate syllable is held somewhat longer and 'to that extent' may be said to carry the main tone, clearly so when the penult is open (ladô, buruăng, pisang), hardly determinable otherwise; speakers differ (kaLAkuan ~ kalaKUan, manDApati ~ mandaPAti, perBANtuan ~ perbanTUan).
229.srule: None: 'de toonsterkte voor iedere lettergreep van een woord... dezelfde... Met dezelfde kracht of gelijk accent op iedere syllabe' - all syllables equal in force, the penult alone slightly longer; no rhythmic or other non-penult prominence described (examples up to five syllables). Later works read (Adelaar 1992:12, 1995:437; Crouch 2009:235) do not mention secondary stress.

morph.rootq: Crouch 2009 p.133: "Affixes, which combine with the root to form a substantive word, are subject to word stress and phrasal stress. However clitics, which include the applicative -an, pronominal enclitics such as -e and -nyo, as well as the passive voice marker di-, do not attract lexical or phrasal stress. There is evidence to suggest that phrasal stress in Minangkabau is syllable final yet clitics are not affected by this tendency. For example, in (159a) stress falls on the final syllable of dimasak ... Notice in (159b) that the applicative clitic -an has been introduced ... Despite this extra phonetic material stress still falls on the -sak syllable." Appendix 2 p.235: "Gil (2006)…
morph.elicq: Crouch 2009 Appendix 2 p.235: "I have conducted a preliminary acoustic study of stress in Minangkabau. The study supports the idea that Minangkabau has phrasal final stress and lend support to Gil's (2006) claims about phrasal stress in Minangkabau. I found that syllables in intonation unit final position were markedly longer and more intense than the same syllable in non-final position. A comparison of the length and intensity of penultimate and word final syllables did not reveal conclusive results. The results from analysis of pitch contours were also inconclusive." contra.head: StressTyp2's coding does not match the source
contra.detail: The database codes initial stress plus an antepenultimate secondary stress, but the one careful primary analysis (Gudava 1969, via Harris §1.3) shows contrastive stress located from the right edge of the word: penultimate in consonant-final words, antepenultimate in vowel-final words. Once that is corrected, the language is no longer a counterexample to Gordon's ranked-constraint typology, nor an attestation of a pattern that only weighted (rather than ranked) constraint grids generate.

qtr.text: 2.1.2. Stress is dynamic (force-based) but weakly expressed. In two- and three-syllable word forms it falls on the initial syllable: skíbu 'millstone', gwéri 'snake', dáčxiri 'fire', dóšurdes 'they got tired'. In polysyllabic words, besides the main stress, associated with the third syllable from the end, a secondary stress (falling on the initial syllable) is also noted: máskilidápari 'healing', méxvamilápiri 'quick-witted'. Elements of vowel harmony occur: cf. dat. uškursu 'to the apple'.

morph.rootq: Kipshidze 1914 §7 (p.013-014): 'Удареніе въ мингрельскомъ, какъ и въ грузинскомъ, стоитъ на второмъ съ конца слогѣ въ двухсложныхъ словахъ и на третьемъ — въ трех- и многосложныхъ: k'óči человѣкъ, osúri женщина, k'óčepi люди, osúrepi женщины, ǰíma братъ, ǰimálepi братья. Однако многосложныя слова наряду съ вышеприведенной формой ударенія имѣютъ и другую, двойную, одно главное удареніе, а другое второстепенное, причемъ четырехсложныя слова дѣлятся поровну 2+2, а пятисложныя — 2+3 съ главнымъ удареніемъ въ началѣ слова … a) Предлоги [= preverbs], равно и частицы, находящіяся впереди глагольной формы и сливающіяся съ ней проклитически, имѣютъ на себѣ главное удареніе: č'ári пиши, dóč'ari…
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined. The nearest indication that the description draws on connected speech rather than citation forms is §7e (p.014): 'Въ вопросительныхъ предложеніяхъ (§ 103) удареніе всегда, независимо отъ числа слоговъ въ словѣ, находится на второмъ съ конца слогѣ, и притомъ удареніе очень сильное, въ то время какъ въ другихъ случаяхъ въ мингрельскомъ удареніе весьма слабое' (together with the remarks on proclitics/enclitics 'въ связной рѣчи' and on verse metre, §157); the grammar is accompanied by a chrestomathy of texts Kipshidze collected in Mingrelia, but he does not say the stress rules were checked against them.
morph.stmt: Mingrelian is exclusively suffixing in the noun (stem + plural -ep- + case, Kipshidze §11: 'въ един. числѣ [окончанія] присоединяются непосредственно къ основамъ, а во множ. числѣ — при посредствѣ показателя множественности -ep-') but mixed in the verb, which follows the common Kartvelian template (Tuite 1998:13, after Deeters 1930): 'slot 1 Preverb … slot 2 Person agreement prefix (Set S or Set O, sometimes both), slot 3 Preradical or version vowel, slot 4 Verb root, slot 5 Passive/inchoative or causative suffix, slot 6 Series marker …, slot 8 Stem suffix, slot 9 Tense/mood vowel, slot 10 Person agreement suffix (Set S), slot 11 Plural suffix' — i.e. preverbs, person prefixes and…

230.cfw: Borise 2020 and Poniava 2020 both report that the placement of Megrelian stress is contested, and the first-hand descriptions disagree on where main stress falls in words longer than two syllables: Kipshidze 1914 gives primary initial stress, Kluge 1916 penultimate, Gudava 1969 a penult/antepenult window for the Senaki dialect with contrastive pairs, Kiria, Ezugbaia, Memishishi and Chukhua 2015 the final vowel, and Poniava 2020's 18-speaker acoustic study initial stress in two- and three-syllable words but second-syllable stress in longer ones, so no single rule has a clear winner.

231.dq: placement of the full-stress syllable which is the center of the phonemic-word is not predictable relative to phonemic-word boundaries. ... With the exception of forms in which certain stressed verbal suffixes occur, the full-stressed syllable, in any TM morphemic-word also constituting a phonemic-word, is the root syllable, or in the case of polysyllabic roots, the first syllable of the root.
231.dloc: Crawford 1963:108 §3.111, scan of the SIL PDF in the copy consulted p.120; p.110 ("This system includes, at the phonemic-word level, three stress units or characteristics--full, reduced, and non-stress") and footnote ("This accentual system also includes two other significant stress levels relevant at the level of phonemic-phrases. These will be discussed in 4.11."); note on the cited source
231.prule: No word-position rule exists at any length. Corrected description: full stress (Crawford's Syllable-type I, the phonemic-word center) falls on the root syllable, or the first syllable of a polysyllabic root; in forms containing the stressed verbal suffixes {váʔan}~/vá·n/ 'desiderative', {kóh} 'again' and {kʌ́hs} 'completely' (which may co-occur), StI is the LAST such suffix syllable and the root plus preceding suffixes of this group tend to carry additional full stress (StII). Word position of StI therefore varies with morphological composition (2-syll: 10, 01, 11, reduced-full all attested; 3-syll: nine variants incl. 100/010/001/110/101), and stress is surface-contrastive (/'apit/ 'thorn' vs /a'pit/ 'rolled up').
231.srule: Besides the one primary (Syllable-type I) stress, a word may carry additional full stresses (Syllable-type II) and reduced stresses (Syllable-type III), placed by morphemic make-up, not rhythm: additional full stresses always precede the primary (the primary is the last full stress in the word) and fall on compounding elements and, in verbs with the stressed suffixes {váʔan}/{kóh}/{kʌ́hs}, on the root and each such suffix before the last (e.g. /nʌ́hkskʌ́skóhɨvá·ndinup/ 'they all want to go again', four full stresses); reduced-stress syllables normally precede the primary. No alternating secondary stress is described.
231.quote: There is in TM a pair of forms /ʔápit/ 'thorn' and /ʔapít/ 'rolled up', which differ only by stress placement. Further evidence of contrastive value of stress is shown by the fact that placement of the full-stress syllable which is the center of the phonemic-word is not predictable relative to phonemic-word boundaries. Thus the center syllable in a phonemic-word (the manifestation of Syllable-type I) may be the first syllable in the phonemic-word, as in cyó·ʔndinuva 'they also left'; it may be the last syllable, as in ʔʌ̀cʌnguhúp 'my hat'; it may occur medially, as in kutǽ·ʔtʌn 'rooster comb'…

The form /ʔápit/ is a polysyllabic root; /ʔapít/ consists of a prefix {ʔa-} plus a root {pít}." p.109: "There are three stressed verbal suffixes ... {váʔan} 'desiderative', {kóh} 'again', and {kʌ́hs} 'completely' ... In forms containing these suffixes, the syllable manifesting Syllable-type I is the last such syllable in the form." Crawford 1965:302: "El acento en mixe de Totontepec es fonémico, pero al…
morph.elicq: Crawford 1963:4 (sec. 0.2): "The present study is based on materials collected by the author ... during the years 1951-57. The materials consist partly of data elicited from informants in citation forms or paradigmatic materials, and partly of connected text. Part of the connected text materials was transcribed directly from informants; a greater part was recorded on magnetic tape. The study of the larger phonological groupings has been based largely on the tape-recorded materials." Cf. p.120: "morphemic units when used as a sample for analysis of phonemic units, consist largely in citation forms or other sorts of single-word sentences."
morph.stmt: Crawford 1965:303: "La estructura de cualquier forma verbal mixe consiste en tres partes principales que son: 1) prefijo indicador de persona, 2) radical y 3) sufijo indicador de aspecto temporal... Encontramos además muchos otros tipos de afijos verbales (sufijos en su mayoría)" - i.e. one obligatory person/possessor prefix slot (plus derivational prefixes yak- causative, tuk-/mu-/cu- applicatives, nay- reflexive, ka- subjunctive) before a root that carries the word stress, with TAM, plural, adverbial and emphatic material suffixed.

231.cfw: Crawford 1963, the one full phonology of Totontepec Mixe, puts main stress on the root syllable and states outright that its position is not predictable from the word edges, and Santos Martínez 2013 finds penultimate or final stress governed by vowel length in the Metepec village of the same language, so the fixed initial-stress rule recorded here comes from a typological database and is stated by neither first-hand description.

233.prule: Accent ('frei-konstant': greater loudness plus higher pitch) mostly on the final syllable ('Meist Oxytona'), more rarely on the penult, sporadically on the antepenult (mostly compound words); constant in verbal inflection: in the present as a rule on the last syllable of a vowel-final verb stem or on the linking vowel after a consonant-final stem, in the perfect forms in -bʌ/-pʌ/-dʃʌ as a rule on the final syllable of the whole form, and in the negative imperative always on the negation bi.
233.srule: Not mentioned in Weiers 1972, Phonetik sec. 3 'Akzent', pp. 89-90 (the section describes one prominent syllable per word and says the syllables following the accent are held accentless; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described).
233.quote: Wir bezeichnen diesen Akzent als zentralisierenden Akzent. Die Stellung dieses zentralisierenden Akzentes ist frei-konstant. Die Akzentfreiheit ergibt sich aus folgendem: Die meisten der überwiegend aus zwei, zuweilen aus drei oder mehr Stammsilben bestehenden Wörter können sein: 1. Meist Oxytona, z.B.: [tʃɔs'un], [dʃɔl'ʌ], [tʃʌʀ'ɔn], [kaʊk'ʌ], [irg'ɔd], [mʊsʊlm'ãn]. 2. Seltener Paroxytona, z.B.: [b'idʌd], [m'ɔnʌd], [tʃʌŋ'ulnɪ], [qur'unɪ], [t'ɛndʌ], [s'unɪ]. 3. Sporadisch Proparoxytona, wobei es sich meist um zusammengesetzte Wörter handelt: [mor'insowʌr], [qʌr'ɔtʃusutu].
233.idn: the Moghol language of the Moghol of the province of Herat, Afghanistan ('Herater-Moghol'); Weiers calls it 'den mongolischen Dialekt der Moghol in Afghanistan'; data: Weiers's own field recordings among the Herat Moghol, made during 'zweimaligen, längeren Aufenthalte' in villages around Herat…
233.exq_: 2. Seltener Paroxytona, z.B.: [b'idʌd], [m'ɔnʌd], [tʃʌŋ'ulnı], [qur'unı], [t'ɛndʌ], [s'unı]. 3. Sporadisch Proparoxytona, wobei es sich meist um zusammengesetzte Wörter handelt ... Beim negativen Imperativ liegt die Betonung stets auf der Negation bi, z.B.: [b'ibɔlʀʌ] „mache nicht!“

morph.rootq: Pritsak 1964:168 §16 'Akzent. — Nach RAMSTEDT (Nr. 5, SS. 55-60) haben folgende Suffixe den Akzent: Plural-Suffixe -ˈūt und -ˈnūt, Nom. perf. -ˈqsōn, Praet. impf. -ˈǰā(n) und Praet. perf. -ˈba. In einigen Fällen ruht der Akzent auf dem Vokal des Stammes (bzw. auf dem Bindevokal) unmittelbar vor dem Suffix: Plural-Suffixe: -z (šāˈnā-z ‘Kämme’), -t (moˈri-t ‘Pferde’); Praes. impf. II -na (iˈr-ȧnȧ ‘er kommt’) und Praes. perf. -lȧ (boˈl-u-lȧ ‘er war’).'
morph.elicq: Pritsak gives the accent facts second-hand from Ramstedt 1906 without saying what they rest on; on Ramstedt's material he says only (p.160 §2): 'Im Herbst 1903 hatte G. J. RAMSTEDT in der russ. mittelasiatischen Festung Kuška ... die Möglichkeit gehabt, ein paar Tage mit einem Mogholen zu arbeiten. Als Produkt dieser Beschäftigung ist 1905 sein Werk „Mogholica” (über 900 Stichwörter und 21 Seiten Texte) erschienen' and (p.161) 'Die vorliegende Skizze basiert im allgemeinen auf dem Material RAMSTEDT's'.
morph.stmt: As Pritsak describes it, Moghol inflection and derivation are suffixal throughout — case, plural, possessive, tense, mood, person, participles, converbs, causative, passive and verbalisers all follow the stem ('Das Kasussuffix steht zwischen dem Stamm und dem Possessivsuffix', §24; compound tenses are built 'indem an die finiten Formen... finite Formen der Hilfsverben a-... oder bi-... hinzugefügt werden', §62); the only grammatical material preceding the verb is the reduced negators lȧ ~ l-, sa ~ s- and prohibitive bi (§38-39), beside heavy Persian influence on syntax and lexicon ('Die Zweisprachigkeit der Mogholen hat besonders stark auf die Syntax eingewirkt', §72).

Die Intensität dieses ... 234.dq: Only one vowel in the word may be stressed. This vowel is often long. No other syllables bear stress. The stressed vowel is usually the penult. Vowels may be inserted to break up inadmissible consonant clusters. This is done after stressing, so that on the surface stress can occur in other positions (eg. the antepenult). Sometimes even a 'dummy' vowel is placed in front of a monosyllabic word to …

Michelson 1988 sec. 3.2 notes only that the first syllable of a word longer than four or five syllables is sometimes more prominent than other unaccented syllables.
234.quote: (2) Mohawk: Prosodic generalizations a. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable (not quantity sensitive) b. A stressed syllable must be heavy (CV: or CVC). c. A word must consist of two syllables. The first generalization (2a) is that Mohawk words have only a single stress, which surfaces on the penultimate syllable. This pattern is shown by the examples in (3-4). ... Stress placement itself does not appear to be quantity-sensitive. The examples given above were chosen to illustrate that stress falls on the penultimate syllable regardless of whether the final syllable is open (3a, 4a), close…

(These vowels were added after the basic penultimate stress pattern of Proto-Northern-Iroquoian was established.) Stressed syllables generally are distinguished by high or rising pitch (á, á:) or rising then plunging pitch (à:)." morph.stmt: Mohawk is polysynthetic and templatic with heavy obligatory prefixation and lighter suffixation: "All verbs contain at least three parts: a pronominal prefix, a verb root, and an aspect suffix... they may contain various prepronominal prefixes (Partitive, Contrastive, Coincident, Negative, Translocative, Factual, Duplicative, Future, Optative, Cislocative, Repetitive)... a Middle, Reflexive, or Reciprocal prefix... an incorporated noun stem. Following the verb root, there may be one or more derivational suffixes (Inchoative, Reversive, Causative, Instrumental Applicative, Benefactive Applicative, Distributive, Purposive). After the aspect suffix, there may be a postaspectual suffix"…

tn.quote: The second respect in which the glottal stop is differentiated from other consonants is by its role in conditioning a falling tone when following a stressed vowel. … Some examples of this process, called LARYNGEAL LENGTHENING by Michelson (1988) and TONE by Postal (1969), are given in (46). (46) a. karù:tats /k-aru÷tat-s/ ‘I blow’ … Notice that the falling tone only occurs on the stressed vowel. If a glottal stop follows an unstressed vowel … no tonal reflex is seen. … I suggest that the falling tone is a phonetic reflex of having a bimoraic vowel whose second mora is shared by a glottal stop

tn.note: A falling tone (with length) appears only on the stressed vowel, before an underlying glottal stop or h+resonant; treated as a predictable reflex rather than a lexical toneme; stress is penultimate.

The grammar was compiled by Hestermann from the missionaries' manuscripts: 'die Spuren der verschiedenen Manuskripte, die mir aus verschiedenen Zeiten und in ganz ungleicher Abfassung, Transkription usw. vorlagen' (Vorwort); no texts were collected ('daß ihn sein früher Tod nicht auch ... zur Zusammenstellung von Texten kommen ließ', Vorwort). Accents are simply printed on cited words and example sentences; the only speech-context remark concerns phrases, not stress: 'Redensarten, welche gleich nach dem Hören niedergeschrieben wurden' (p.136).

237.prule: Primary stress falls uniformly on the word-initial syllable (Walker 1996: 31, reporting Kenstowicz after Tsygankin & Debaev 1975).
237.srule: Not mentioned in the deciding chain (Walker 1996 ROA-172: 31; Kenstowicz 1994 ROA-33: 4-7). First-hand descriptions give a rule: in words of three or more syllables an additional (secondary) stress falls on alternate syllables, forming disyllabic feet - typically the odd-numbered syllables (1st and 3rd: śed́ejsenze 'in his/her heart'), or the even-numbered ones (2nd and 4th) when sentence rhythm shifts the stress; trisyllabic feet occur less often (Aasmäe 2014: 13; Aasmäe 2006: 17-18, 33-34; Aasmäe 2015: 19).
237.quote: A similar effect takes place in the contrast between the stress patterns of the Erzyan and Mokshan dialects of Mordwin. Kenstowicz (1995: 31) notes that according to Tsygankin and DeBaev (1975) the Erzyan dialect has uniformly initial stress, While the Mokshan dialect stresses the leftmost strong syllable else leftmost syllable. Kenstowicz analyzes this as the Erzyan dialect simply reranking the left alignment constraint above PK-PROM, so that satisfying alignment supercedes the preference of stressing a strong vowel.
237.loc: p. 31 (in sec. 2.5 'Default-to-opposite-side systems with nonfinality', last paragraph on the page, after the Eastern Cheremis rankings (68)); held text

morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: 'In the case of derivation, a suffix is added to the word stem, e.g. ašo "white", ašińe "white (diminutive)", ašolgadoms "to become white"' (Aasmäe 2014: 17); 'Though the word stem can be followed by several suffixes, e.g.: moravtińďeŕasamiź "in case they ask us to sing"...' (Aasmäe 2006: 19); 'nominal inflection can, roughly speaking, be broken into three linear-ordered groups of affixes expressing: (i) the categories and notions of case, number and definiteness...; (ii) nominal conjugation, and (iii) the clitic' (Rueter 2010: 74) — all post-stem; the only pre-verbal grammatical markers are free negative words (a, eź-, iĺa, apak, avoĺ).

238.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; words ending in the glottal stop or a nasalized plosive (coda /k p t/) are stressed on the final syllable; disyllabic Spanish loans with original final stress keep it (/sen'jor/, /mo'tor/); disyllabic internal clitics usually stay unstressed, leaving stress on the base-final (antepenultimate) syllable of the word form.
238.srule: Secondary stress in morphologically complex words: a base that can occur as an independent word retains its stress as secondary when further morphemes are added (compounds, derived words), main stress being penultimate in the whole word; Haude says the exact conditions require further research and does not mark it. No quantity-insensitive rhythmic secondary.
238.quote: Stress normally occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. In (161) and (162), this can be seen from the fact that when a word is augmented, stress shifts to the right: (161) /a'waro/ ... ‘parrot’ /awa'ro:di/ ... ‘little parrot’ ... Only on words ending the glottal stop or in a nasalized plosive (cf. 2.3.1), stress falls on the last syllable: (163) ... /bakwan'jit/ ... ‘underarm’ ... /pa:kona:'nak/ ... ‘fox’ The presence or absence of the release vowel after a glottal stop (cf. 2.3.2) does not influence the stress pattern: (164) /me'rek/ ... ‘big’
238.idn: Movima; data: Haude 2006: own elicitation and text data from four field trips to Santa Ana del Yacuma (Beni Department, Bolivia) between 2001–2004, about nine months in total; Haude 2023: 'spoken in and around Santa Ana del Yacuma'; Judy & Judy 1962: 'la region de Santa Ana del departamento del Beni', data collected…
238.exq_: Only on words ending the glottal stop or in a nasalized plosive ..., stress falls on the last syllable: /tʃu:'hat/, /pa:kona:'nak/ (p.46). When the last syllable of a Spanish word is stressed, the original stress is retained in disyllabic, but not in longer loans: /sen'jor/, /mo'tor/ (p.50).

238.sec_rule: Secondary stress is morphologically conditioned: an element that can occur as an independent word keeps its own (penultimate) stress as a secondary stress inside compounds and other complex words (e.g. /iti'la:kwa/ 'man' within /itilakwa-n-di'tʃi:je/ 'little boy'; the first member of a compound 'only receives secondary stress'); it is lost only when a monosyllabic unstressed element is attached. 'The exact conditions for the assignment of secondary stress require further research'; Haude does not transcribe it. No rhythmic secondary stress described.
238.sec_quote: The assignment of secondary stress is more complicated. Here, the morphological properties of the word play a role. In principle, a word which can occur independently retains its stress pattern also when combined with other morphemes. [...] The exact conditions for the assignment of secondary stress require further research. [...] I do not represent secondary stress.

The long-short distinction with vowels is only ever made in stressable syllables, and then only rarely in any syllable but the first. Thus, we find: /ðúʔu/ 'yamstick' /pá:na/ 'level' /kálipwa/ 'gully' /árana/ 'toenail, fingernail' /dʳé:gwati/ 'trevally' /bwáʔa/ 'meat' /ʔúnuwána/ 'blister' /máɣuʔí:ni/ 'mullet' Note however that if an otherwise stressable syllable is the last of a word, it is not stressed. 2.4 MORPHOPHONEMICS ...

Thus, we find: /ðú?u/ 'yamstick', /pá:na/ 'level', /kálipwa/ 'gully', /árana/ 'toenail, fingernail', /dré:gwati/ 'trevally', /bwá?a/ 'meat', /?únuwána/ 'blister', /máɣu?í:ni/ 'mullet'. Note however that if an otherwise stressable syllable is the last of a word, it is not stressed."

239.heavy: Nothing is counted as heavy for stress placement. The only weight-related statement runs the other way: the vowel long-short distinction 'is only ever made in stressable syllables, and then only rarely in any syllable but the first' (length is licensed by the odd-numbered stressable positions, e.g. /máɣuʔí:ni/ with the long vowel in stressed syllable 3), i.e. stress conditions length, not length stress.
239.dflt: not applicable (weight plays no role); initial
239.prule: Stress on the first syllable and every alternate (odd-numbered) syllable thereafter, counting from the left; an otherwise stressable syllable that is word-final is not stressed (/kálipwa/ 1 only; /ʔúnuwána/, /máɣuʔí:ni/ 1 and 3). Crowley marks all stresses with the same acute and does not rank them; StressTyp2/Gordon read the initial as main stress.
239.srule: Every alternate (odd-numbered) syllable after the first, counting from the left, is also stressed, but a word-final syllable never is: 3-syllable /kálipwa/ stressed on syllable 1 only, 4-syllable /ʔúnuwána/, /máɣuʔí:ni/ on syllables 1 and 3 (Crowley writes these with the same acute as the initial stress and does not call them secondary; 'secondary' is StressTyp's/Hayes 1995's label).

morph.rootq: §2.3 STRESS (pp.155-156): 'The Anguthimri stress pattern is as follows: (C)V́(C)CV(C)CV́(C)CV... i.e. the first syllable and every alternate syllable receives stress. The long-short distinction with vowels is only ever made in stressable syllables, and then only rarely in any syllable but the first. ... Note however that if an otherwise stressable syllable is the last of a word, it is not stressed.' The rule is stated over the word from its first syllable; no mention of root, stem or affixes. (Only indirect morphological remark, §3.2.1(viii) p.167: the desiderative -kVd̪a: 'is the only source for words in the language containing long vowels in a syllable other than the first'.)
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined. in §2.3; the pattern is illustrated only by eight isolated citation-form nouns: 'Thus, we find: /ðúʔu/ 'yamstick', /pá:na/ 'level', /kálipwa/ 'gully', /árana/ 'toenail, fingernail', /dʳé:gwati/ 'trevally', /bwáʔa/ 'meat', /ʔúnuwána/ 'blister', /máɣuʔí:ni/ 'mullet''. Context elsewhere: 'The present study of the Mpakwithi dialect of Anguthimri is a salvage study only.... The only known speaker of the Mpakwithi dialect today, Mr. Don Fletcher...' (§1.6 p.151) and 'Note that in elicitation, nouns are always cited with no suffix.' (§3.2.1 p.163).
morph.stmt: Crowley 1981 §1.1 (p.147): 'Like all of the languages of Cape York Peninsula (and indeed, the rest of Queensland), it is a wholly suffixing language.... There is no pronominal incorporation in the verb.' All inflection (nominal case, verbal tense/imperative/consecutive) and all derivation (proprietive, privative, diminutive, plural, genitive; causative, inchoative, reflexive, reciprocal) are suffixes; negation, demonstratives and pronouns are free words; reduplication is marginal.

Ultimately we had some 75 texts of varying lengths at our disposal.'
morph.stmt: Muna is mixed but prefix-heavy: person inflection is split — 'the obligatory presence of the prefixes marking subject inflection' on every verb (§3.3.2 p.45) versus direct/indirect-object and possessive marking by suffixes (§4.8, §5.4.1) — while derivation, 'the most complicated and widely used process' with 'affixes... further subdivided into prefixes, suffixes, infixes and circumfixes' (Ch.10 p.275), is dominated by prefixes: of the 51 affixes/affix-combinations in the §10.1 summary chart (pp.277-278) about 33 are prefixes or prefix+reduplication (causative fo-/feka-, nominalizer ka-, ko- 'have', po- reciprocal, ti- passive, habitual ngko-, etc.), 11 are suffixes…

contra.head: StressTyp2 codes a fixed pattern that its source does not state
contra.detail: StressTyp2 codes initial primary stress with alternating secondaries from the left, after Street & Mollinjin 1981 (cited via Gordon 2002), who give initial primary stress with further stresses on odd-numbered syllables but also morphologically conditioned alternative patterns for polymorphemic words ('no simple rules can be formulated'). The first-hand description cited here, Mansfield 2019, finds no acoustic correlates for any of the earlier stress proposals and doubts that the language has word stress at all, identifying only a phrase-level penultimate pitch accent. The language is therefore not listed under fixed stress.

contra.head: StressTyp2's coding does not match the source
contra.detail: Mansfield 2014:176-181: in three-syllable words stress varies lexically between the first and second syllable; in four-syllable words primary stress falls on the third syllable; five-syllable words are footed (ˌσσ)(ˈσσσ), i.e. secondary stress on the first syllable and primary on the third. There is no stress on final odd-numbered syllables and primary stress is not initial, so Murinbata leaves the pattern class.

241.dq: There is exactly one pitch accent in each PPhrase, predictably anchored to the penultimate syllable of the right-most PWord within the PPhrase. [...] However not all PWords have accents, as multiple PWords combining into a PPhrase have just one accent, on the right-most PWord.
241.quote: I have not been able to find acoustic correlates to support any of the earlier proposals for stress in Murrinhpatha ... I therefore propose that Murrinhpatha probably does not have any metrical grid of alternating stressed syllables. ... The only systematic form of prominence that I have identified is the pitch accent anchored to the penultimate syllable ... The Murrinhpatha prosodic system therefore has no lexical contrasts, but rather has a demarcative function triangulating the boundary of PWord and PPhrase constituents ... The system is similar to that of French, which is also analysed as…
241.idn: Murrinhpatha (also spelled Murrinh Patha), including examples from speakers across the Wadeye community; Murrinh Kura mentioned as 'a variety of Murrinhpatha' but not separately described; data: Wadeye (Port Keats), Daly region, northern Australia; author's own c. 50 hours of recordings plus corpora shared by…
241.exq_: Finally, it is worth noting that some English loanwords introduce word-final accentual anchoring, breaking the general Murrinhpatha pattern of penultimate accent (75) (§4.3). 241.cfw: Mansfield's 2019 grammar, building on his 2017 acoustic study, finds no metrical word stress in Murrinhpatha but only a pitch accent on the penultimate syllable of the phrase-final prosodic word, whereas the older impressionistic descriptions of Walsh 1976, Street and Mollinjin 1981 and Blythe 2009 place primary stress on the first syllable and disagree with one another about secondary stresses.

morph.rootq: "Strong stress (marked by ´) occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word (see also 2.3.4.1.2): /mamatoy/ [mamátoy] 'will kill' /potoyon/ [potóyon] 'will be killed'" (§2.2.1.1 p.14), where "A word is an utterance consisting of one free morpheme and any affixes attached to it" and "A bound morpheme or affix is an unstressed, usually monosyllabic morpheme" (§2.1 p.13); weak stress "occurs on the first syllable of the word when it is separated from the strong stress by two or more syllables: /pamamagambad/ [pàmamagámbar] 'camera'" (§2.2.1.2). The domain is the affixed word, not the root (potoy-on shifts stress onto the root-final syllable).
morph.elicq: Stress section gives no explicit evidence statement, but it covers phrase-level behaviour ("Weak stress ... (2) replaces strong stress in a word which is subordinate to another within a phrase: /mapulak abuk/ '(the) white-haired (one)'" §2.2.1.2 p.14) as well as isolated words; the data statement is §1.2.3 p.8: "Material was obtained by direct eliciting of noun-lists and short sentences grouped in semantic domains ... Textual material was obtained either a) by presenting the informant sentence by sentence with an imaginary (but plausible) dialogue for translation ...; b) by asking him to relate a folk-tale ...; or c) by recording a spontaneous conversation".
morph.stmt: Predominantly prefixing-infixing with a small set of heavily used suffixes: "A total of 60 derivational morphemes has been recorded, consisting of 53 prefixes, four infixes and three suffixes" (§5.1 p.114); verbal inflection combines mode/aspect prefixes (ma-, na-, pa-, ka-, ki-, ti-, N-/g-) and the infixes -um-/-in- with focus suffixes -on/-in/-an/-ʔ (§5.2.1 p.130), while nominal determiners, plural markers and possessive/subject pronouns are post-head clitics and case relation markers are preposed particles.

morph.stmt: Miskito is head-final and almost entirely suffixing: verbal tense-aspect, subject person, mood (imperative, 'conexivo'), negation (-ras), the noun construct state and 1st/2nd-person possessor (-ka, -i, -m; infixed -i-/-m- in relational nouns), the case enclitic =ra and every derivational process (-ka, -ra, -s, -ni, -k-/-b-/-w-) follow the root -- Salamanca's schema for derivation is "X+m--->Y... y 'm' es un morfema, generalmente un sufijo" (p.192) and he notes the "extrema monotonía" of the same few suffixes recurring (p.224); the only pre-root material is the 3rd-person/1st-inclusive possessive 'prefijo o clítico' ai-/wan-, the reflexive/detransitivising prefix ai-, the preverbal object…

244.cfw: Salamanca's 1988 MIT grammar and his 2008 overview, independently backed by the CIDCA grammar Miskitu Bila Aisanka (1985), put main stress on the first syllable with only a few listed exceptions (aisabé, umpira, sakuna); the only dissent is Morales Quant, Padilla Brown and Zapata Webb's 2007 orthography study, which claims a second stress class on the second syllable but rests largely on those same exception words, and Constenla's 1987 passing opinion that Miskito is tonal, which Salamanca 2008 flatly denies.

morph.rootq: The grammar gives no word-stress or accent rule. The only mention of stress is definitional, in the syllable section (p.59): 'A syllable includes not only the sequential phonemes but also prosodic features like stress, tone etc.'; and on p.49: 'All the vowels are voiced and the tone is not a phonemic feature.' No statement locates stress relative to root, stem, or word edge.
morph.elicq: No stress description exists in the source, so no elicitation context can be quoted. (For the texts used for tokens, the source states, p.183: 'The folktales in each Naga language were translated into Naga Pidgin by the informat concerned. Later all the stories were re-written by this writer to fit in with the system of the standardised grammar of Naga Pidgin presented in the body of this book.')
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing/postposing: 'depending upon whether or not a word/stem is capable of taking a suffix, the words/stems in this language can be primarily divided into two, viz., variables and invariables. The variables form a class of words which are capable of taking suffixes' (§3.1 p.73); nouns are 'N = Root ± plural + case' (p.80) and verbs 'Root + tense/modal' (p.106), with case postpositions, definite/inclusive/emphatic particles and modal auxiliaries all following their host; the only pre-verbal grammatical element is the negative particle nə (no-jabi 'do not go').

morph.elicq: The stress section consists solely of "Stress is penultimate. The very rare exceptions are marked with an accent (´)." (p.6); no statement of the evidence base. The Introduction says only that the sketch draws on five years of study, the Brewers' Vocabulario Mexicano de Tetelcingo and "a concordance of texts collected by them" (p.5).
morph.stmt: Tuggy's OVERALL VERB STRUCTURE (p.116): "Pre-Stem Elements: PAST - SM - OM - [DIRL/ADV] - UNSPEC OM - STEM... Post-Stem Elements: STEM - CAUS - APPLIC (several) - [3P HON or HON REFL] - ASP - TNS" -- i.e. person (subject, object, reflexive, unspecified-object) and the optional PAST o- are prefixed, while all derivation (causative, applicative, verbalizers, nominalizers), honorific, aspect, tense and number marking are suffixed; nouns take possessor prefixes but absolutive, plural, possessed-plural, diminutive/augmentative and locative suffixes.

contra.head: The published descriptions contradict each other
contra.detail: Gordon 2002 (coding Hagman 1977) and Hahn 1870 sec. 8 give word-initial (stem) stress, Hahn inside a three-tone description; Planert 1905:109 says the accent falls now on the stem, now on the suffix, and rejects F. Müller's account of the accent; Brugman 2009 (pp. 28, 88) states that Khoekhoe has no stress, and Haacke (1992) treats its word prosody as lexical tone only. The record codes the kind as an unresolved conflict and quotes both sides.

248.prule: Two readings, unresolved. (a) Initial stress: Gordon 2002 appendix p. 542 'Initial (mora)' (survey coding from Hagman 1977, not seen); Hahn 1870 sec. 8 p. 24: the accent stays on the monosyllabic stem, hence on the first syllable, with compound and reduplication-plus-suffix exceptions, stated inside a description of a threefold word tone (sec. 7, p. 23). (b) No word stress: Brugman 2009 (Cornell PhD, instrumental) p. 28 'Khoekhoe lacks both stress and segmental alternations', p. 88 'Khoekhoe has no stress, segment or tone alternations'; Haacke's UCL thesis (1992) analyses Khoekhoe word prosody as lexical tone (four tonemes, two per bimoraic root) and does not treat word stress; Planert 1905:109 had already rejected a fixed stem accent ('betont bald die Stammsilbe, bald das Suffix').
248.srule: None reported: Gordon 2002 codes Nama as a single-stress (fixed initial) language, i.e. one stress per word with no secondary or rhythmic stresses (survey coding from Hagman 1977, not seen); Hahn 1870 sec. 8 gives one accent per word and mentions no secondary accent; Brugman 2009 (pp.28, 88) finds no word stress at all.

tn.quote: Arguments are presented in favour of a register system as opposed to a contour system, i.e. that a tonal melody consists of a sequence of two level tonemes. In addition to the six major citation melodies and their sandhi versions, some residual melodies are identified, which are due to former depressor segments. ... It has been shown that lexical tone in Khoekhoe is based on a bimoraic foot, and that each melody must be analyzed in terms of two tonemes out of a set of four. ... For practical purposes only four surface tonemes need to be recognized, however, bacause of partial overlap.
tn.cite: Haacke, Wilfrid H. G. 1992. The tonology of Khoekhoe (Nama/Damara). PhD thesis, University College London (ProQuest 10044439; publ. Koeln: Koeppe).
tn.locator: Abstract (front matter, unpaginated)... ch. 5 Conclusion, p.266
tn.note: Four level tonemes, two per bimoraic root, give six main lexical melodies (plus rare residual ones), each with a citation and a sandhi form; rises and falls are tone sequences. Word stress untreated. Checked against the source (tone consistency check round 3, 2026-09-24): domain every syllable -> stem or root (sec.2.1.2; p.266 ch.5 Conclusion; p.235 sec.4.1.1; p.31 sec.2.2).

corr.words: These tonemes combine into a pair (foot) on (disyllabic) roots to form six "tonal profiles" - which, for the sake of conformity, will be referred to as (tonal) melodies henceforth. ... lexical tone in Khoekhoe is based on a bimoraic foot ... These tones are stable, i.e. they are not sensitive to the tone of a preceding stem. In turn they also do not affect the melody of the stem.
corr.loc: sec.2.1.2; p.266 ch.5 Conclusion; p.235 sec.4.1.1; p.31 sec.2.2

248.cfw: Brugman 2009, the only modern first-hand phonology of Khoekhoe consulted, states outright that the language has no word stress and that word prosody is tonal, while the initial-stress coding rests on Gordon 2002's survey line citing Hagman 1977 and on Hahn 1870, whose 'accent' sits inside a three-tone description and which Planert 1905 already contradicted with a stem-or-suffix rule.

qtr.text: Intensity accent [word stress] is phonemic. The root always receives the primary stress. It is not marked in the orthography because the cases in which a native speaker would not know where the root ends and the suffix system begins are few. In this section (24) stress will be marked with an apostrophe before the stressed syllable in the Nambikuara examples. In the other sections it will not be marked.

dqtr.text: The intensity accent [stress] is phonemic. The root always receives the primary stress. This is not marked in the orthography because the cases in which a native speaker would not know where the root ends and the suffix system begins are few.

249.prule: None exists. No quantity-insensitive pattern is codable at any length: the primary source states stress is phonemic and root-anchored, and its examples attest two or three different positions at every length 3-6, none of them final. The language exits as lexical (Kroeker 2003:111, §24.4); the coded all-lengths-final row (01 001 0001 00001 000001 0000001 00000001) is retired, not replaced.
249.srule: Kroeker 2003 gives no placement: only 'a raiz recebe sempre o acento principal' (§24.4 p. 111), with a second stress marked on a suffix syllable in exx. (437) 'na¹kxai²'nãn²-tu³ and (438) 'Na¹-'tu¹wa² (p. 115) and no rule. Mendes Costa 2020: secondary stress (cued by vowel duration) falls on lexically stressed grammatical morphemes near the root — affix stress is lexical, partly predictable by weight (classifiers with a heavy syllable always stressed; peripheral tense/evidential/aspect suffixes never) — on the first root of a two-root word, and on a second heavy syllable inside the base; adjacent stresses allowed; not iterative or alternating. Marques 2022 reports the same for Sararé.
249.quote: O acento de intensidade é fonêmico. A raiz recebe sempre o acento principal. Este não é marcado na ortografia por serem poucos os casos quando um falante nativo não iria saber onde termina a raiz e começa o sistema de sufixos. Nesta seção (24), o acento de intensidade será marcado com apóstrofo antes da sílaba acentuada nos exemplos nambikuara. Nas demais seções não será marcado.
249.idn: 'a língua nambikuara' as a whole: Kroeker treats all Nambikuara groups (Guaporé valley: ha³hãi¹te²su², a³lãn¹te²su², wai²ki³su², wa³su³su², ka³ti³tµu³lhu²; Juruena/Parecis plateau: ne³su², si³wxai³su², ki³thãu³lhu², sax³wen³te²su², ha³lo²te²su², wa³ka³li³te²su²) as mutually intelligible dialect variants of one…
249.exq_: O acento de intensidade é fonêmico. A raiz recebe sempre o acento principal.
249.tone: Tone language: every syllable carries one of three phonemic tones (¹ falling, ² rising, ³ low level), independent of nasalization and laryngealization (Kroeker 2003:110-111 §24.3; Introdução p. 5 'Sendo uma língua tonal'). The 'acento de intensidade' (stress) is a separate phonemic prominence, always on the root (§24.4, p. 111), and conditions length: the stressed syllable is always longer (§24.5).

morph.elicq: No statement of how stress placement was determined. §24 intro p.107: 'Todos os exemplos da seção 24 mostram a acentuação com apóstrofo antes da sílaba. Os demais segmentos não marcam a acentuação.' The stress-marked examples (§§24.3-24.7, pp.110-116) are isolated words and one- or two-word sentences. General data basis, Introdução p.4: 'A base deste estudo é formada de mais de 1.500 páginas de textos gravados e transcritos' and the author 'tem morado durante muitos anos em aldeias nambikuara, falando a língua diariamente.'
morph.stmt: Introdução p.4: 'É uma língua aglutinante, com a maior parte da informação carregada por sufixos à raiz verbal e, em grau menor, por sufixos à raiz nominativa'; §18.1 p.73: 'Existem certos afixos derivacionais, – prefixos e sufixos – e um número bem maior de sufixos flexionais na raiz verbal' — i.e. overwhelmingly suffixing (verb template INSTL + Root + ME BN ADV1 O.PES ADV2 S.PES.PL NEG AUX S.1SG T/E ASP CLT; noun template POS + Root + CC GR EC MT DEM CLT.N ART), the only prefixes being nominal possessor prefixes and the five verbal instrumental/causative prefixes.

dfl.pattern: primary source (Kroeker 2003) states no default position beyond 'the root always receives primary stress'. Mendes Costa 2020 states the position inside the...
dfl.note: primary source (Kroeker 2003) states no default position beyond 'the root always receives primary stress'. Mendes Costa 2020 states the position inside the root: the heavy (branching-rhyme) syllable of the root; if all root syllables are heavy or all light, the RIGHTMOST root syllable (root-final default), with root-final light /i/ syllables extrametrical.
dfl.q: A língua é sensível ao peso silábico no que se refere à atribuição do acento e, sendo assim, é na sílaba pesada da base que o mesmo se fará presente. Caso todas as sílabas sejam pesadas ou leves, o acento é marcado na sílaba mais à direita, cumprindo-se, então, o terceiro parâmetro supramencionado: posição da sílaba.
dfl.c: Mendes Costa, Paula. 2020. Fonologia segmental e suprassegmental do Nambikwara do Campo (Nambikwara do Sul). Tese de doutorado, UFPE, Recife. xvi+418 pp.

vlen.q: A extensão é sempre previsível, com base na acentuação e composição das sílabas. A sílaba acentuada é sempre mais comprida. Sendo aberta a sílaba, a vogal é mais comprida. Sendo fechada a sílaba, a última consoante é mais comprida.

tones: ³ tom grave (registro grave, low level)
tn.quote: Cada sílaba deve ser marcada por um dos três tons fonêmicos. Há um tom de registro grave, um glide ascendente e um glide decrescente. São marcados na ortografia prática pelos números de índice superior ¹, ² e ³. Indicam respectivamente tom decrescente, ascendente e grave. Funcionam independentemente da nasalização e da laringalização. ... O acento de intensidade é fonêmico. A raiz recebe sempre o acento principal.
tn.translation: Every syllable must be marked with one of the three phonemic tones. There is a low register tone, a rising glide and a falling glide. They are marked in the practical orthography by the superscript numbers 1, 2 and 3. These indicate respectively falling, rising and low tone. They function independently of nasalization and laryngealization. ... The intensity accent [stress] is phonemic. The root always receives the primary stress.
tn.cite: Kroeker, Menno H. 2003. Gramática descritiva da língua Nambikuara. Cuiabá: Sociedade Internacional de Lingüística (traduzido do original em inglês, A Descriptive Grammar of Nambikuara, IJAL 67(1), January 2001).
tn.locator: pp. 110-111, sec. 24.3 'Tom' and sec. 24.4 'Acento de intensidade'
tn.note: Three phonemic tones on every syllable (falling, rising, low), shown by a minimal triplet; phonemic root stress stated separately; grammatical tone perturbation on verb roots; nothing on downstep.

249.cfw: Kroeker 2001 and the two modern phonology dissertations, Mendes Costa 2020 on Nambikwara do Campo and Marques 2022 on Sararé, all put main stress on the root rather than on a fixed word-edge syllable and differ only on whether the stressed syllable inside the root is contrastive (Kroeker) or predictable from syllable weight with a rightmost default (Mendes Costa, Marques), while the only final-stress claim is StressTyp2's entry taken from a passage of Price 1976 that StressTyp2's own note calls unreliable.

qtr.text: Nanai vowel reduction has no such link with stress as in Russian. It depends entirely on the order of syllables in the word: in initial syllables vowels are not reduced at all, in medial syllables they are reduced, as a rule, weakly, and in final syllables they are reduced most often and most strongly. Thus the vowels most subject to reduction turn out to be the vowels under stress, since the latter always falls, in Nanai words, on the final syllable. ... As to its place in the word, Nanai stress is strictly regular, bound: it always falls on the last syllable of the word, regardless of its m…

250.srule: Avrorin 1959: 63 tentatively ('по-видимому') posits, besides the main final stress, an additional weak dynamic stress on the last syllable of the stem in polysyllabic words with inflectional suffixes, and on the tense suffix in participles, adding that 'the presence and character of the additional stress require instrumental verification'. His 1968 sketch (§ 4, p. 131) instead lists 'a single stress on the last syllable' (единое ударение на последнем слоге) among the phonetic marks of the word.
250.quote: Такой связи с ударением, как в русском языке, нанайская редукция гласных не имеет. Она целиком зависит от порядка следования слогов в слове: в начальных слогах гласные вовсе не редуцируются, в срединных слогах гласные редуцируются, как правило, слабо, а в конечных слогах редуцируются чаще всего и сильнее всего. Таким образом, наиболее подверженными редукции оказываются гласные под ударением, поскольку последнее всегда в нанайских словах падает на конечный слог. ... morph.rootq: Avrorin 1959 t.1 p.62-63: 'По месту в слове нанайское ударение является строго регулярным, связанным — оно всегда падает на последний слог слова, независимо от его морфологической структуры. Оно оказывается на последнем слоге не только тогда, когда слово включает в свой состав ряд суффиксов, но даже и тогда, когда в состав слова включается одна, а иногда и две-три суффиксальные частицы.' ... 'По-видимому, кроме этого главного ударения, в нанайском языке имеется еще и дополнительное слабое силовое ударение (уступающее по силе главному), которое в многосложных, оформленных словоизменительными суффиксами словах падает на последний слог основы, а у причастий — на временной суффикс. ... Однако…
morph.elicq: Avrorin 1959 t.1 p.62: 'вопрос об ударении остается до сих пор одним из наименее изученных вопросов нанайской фонетики, ожидающим в первую очередь своего экспериментально-инструментального исследования. ... Особенно отчетливо музыкальный (тонический) характер ударения выявляется при изолированном произношении отдельных слов, прежде всего при употреблении отдельных слов в целях наименования отдельных предметов и явлений или при обращении.' (auditory/impressionistic, no frames or measurements; the modern minlang sketch adds: 'Отсутствует контрастивное силовое ударение. ... последний слог при воздействии фразовой просодии удлиняется'.)
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: 'все формальные морфемы располагаются в слове после корня. Нанайская морфология не знает ни префиксов, ни инфиксов, она оперирует только суффиксами' (Avrorin 1959 t.1: 83); 'нанайский язык может быть определен как агглютинативно-суффиксальный' (Avrorin 1968: 132); minlang sketch: 'Словоформа глагола и имени представляет из себя корень, за которым следует около 27 позиций для служебных морфем (не считая энклитик). Префиксации нет, нет редупликации с грамматическим значением.'

tn.quote: По своему характеру нанайское ударение может быть определено скорее всего как смешанное — музыкально-силовое. Основной его особенностью является некоторое повышение тона ударного гласного, выделяющее последний из числа остальных более низких по тону гласных звуков слова. ... Однако повышение тона ударного гласного сопровождается и некоторым силовым напряжением, правда, очень незначительным. ... По месту в слове нанайское ударение является строго регулярным, связанным — оно всегда падает на последний слог слова, независимо от его морфологической структуры.
tn.translation: In its character Nanai stress can most likely be defined as mixed — musical-dynamic. Its main feature is a certain raising of the tone of the stressed vowel, which sets the latter apart from the remaining, lower-toned vowels of the word. ... However, the raising of the tone of the stressed vowel is also accompanied by some intensity, though very slight. ... As to its place in the word, Nanai stress is strictly regular, bound — it always falls on the last syllable of the word, regardless of its morphological structure.
tn.cite: Avrorin, V. A. 1959. Grammatika nanajskogo jazyka, t. 1: Fonetičeskoe vvedenie i morfologija imennyx častej reči. Moskva-Leningrad: Izd. AN SSSR.
tn.note: No lexical tone. Avrorin calls the fixed final word stress 'musical-dynamic': a slight pitch rise on the last vowel with very weak intensity; not contrastive; he says it awaits instrumental study.

For example: ána 'child', aná-mu 'your child' ... mánu 'chicken', manú-na 'his chicken'.

253.heavy: The source states no 'heavy'/'weight' criterion (no long-vowel or closed-syllable condition). What perturbs the count is vowel quality: syllables whose nucleus is the 'schwa' (Salminen's reduced vowel °) are never stressed, and any syllable immediately preceding a schwa syllable is stressed even directly after a stressed syllable. Nikolaeva 2014:18 on °: 'its underlying presence has suprasegmental effects: basically, it adds a mora to the preceding segment... This vowel does not occur in the first syllable and is never stressed.' StressTyp2 recasts this as 'CV(C) followed by C@ count as heavy together'.
253.dflt: initial primary; further stresses on non-final odd-numbered syllables from the left
253.prule: Primary stress on the leftmost syllable whose nucleus is not the schwa (°): the initial syllable in all native words (the schwa 'is practically absent in the first syllable'); in a few loanwords with an initial-syllable schwa (p°rasyin°, t°ronyi, x°ryís°tya) 'The primary stress is then on the next syllable.'
253.srule: Further stresses on non-final odd-numbered syllables counting from the initial (primary-stressed) syllable ('the first syllable of each two-syllable string is stressed, or in other words, the stress falls on non-final odd syllables'), with the schwa ° overriding the count: a syllable containing ° is never stressed and the syllable immediately preceding a ° syllable is stressed even directly after a stressed syllable; the final syllable is unstressed. Salminen calls all of these 'stress' (he does not use the term 'secondary').

tn.quote: We assume that the words in Tundra Nenets can be either lexically accented or unaccented. Lexically unaccented words are the ones that obey the generalization stated above: they have the pitch rise through the first two moras. On the contrary lexically accented words have a prelinked tone on one of the first two syllables in their lexical specification. … The presence of stems with lexically prelinked high tone creates the possibility of tonal minimal pairs. … Stress system of Tundra Nenets can be generally characterized as a pitch accent system with word-initial lengthening.

253.cfw: Salminen's grammatical sketch (1998, revised 2012) and Nikolaeva's grammar (2014) analyse Tundra Nenets stress as predictable and initial, but Amelina's instrumental studies of the Yamal, Kanin and Gydan dialects (2011, 2012) find mobile, contrastive stress on the second syllable in about half of two-syllable nouns, siding with Tereshchenko (1965) and Popova (1966, 1978), while Staroverov (2006) measures initial lengthening in the Malaya Zemlya dialect together with a lexical pitch accent, so the very type of the system is under active debate.

morph.rootq: §1.1 p.1: 'In Nengone, stress is non-phonemic. It has only the demarcative function of indicating the division between words. ... (a) Primary Stress: In words of more than one syllable, the primary stress always falls on the penultimate syllable. (b) Secondary Stress: The secondary stress always occurs two syllables before the primary stress. (c) Unstress: All syllable Nuclei not covered by (a) and (b) are unstressed.' The rule is stated over the word's syllables; root, stem and affixes are not mentioned.
morph.elicq: No method is stated. The stress section is illustrated only with isolated citation words sorted by length: 'EXAMPLES: ... Words of one syllable: /čo/ Future tense marker; /ke/ but. Words of two syllables: /moma/ old man; /yawe/ again. Words of three syllables: /newata/ toe nail; /wabuyu/ thighs. Words of four syllables: /waegogo/ eye ... Words of five syllables: /anititini/ to growl; /wačaruwiwi/ eel.' (p.1). Preface: 'This monograph is based on linguistic material collected during fieldwork in the Loyalty Islands ... May to December 1965, and in July 1966.' The appendix texts are labelled 'unelicited' but carry no stress marks.
morph.stmt: Tryon gives no one-line typological label; his description shows all inflection-like categories (tense/aspect 'Time particles' či/čo/ŋa/ha, negator deko, articles, subject/object pronouns, imperative lu/lo) as free words placed before the verb or noun head, while bound morphology is confined to word-formation (§4 'Word Level Analysis', pp.82-85): 'Causative Verb: +Prefix (a) + Verb Stem + Suffix (-ni)', accompanying e-, reciprocal e-…-keu, restricted reciprocal i-, transitivising suffix -on/-n, verbaliser a-…-ni, adverbial -on, quantity-noun -il, noun-forming ŋa-, and 'Many words are composed of an affix plus free morpheme' (ača-, ada-, aŋa-, gu-, ie-, tube-, wa- — all prefixes, §4.4)…

StressTyp2 record: LECT 728 entry "Stress is largely penultimate, but there are many exceptions. In words of more than 3 syllables there are many competing patterns (Merlan 1983)" + PD words 1883-1891. Owner note: "Domain: word. Merlan's terms are 'word-stress' and 'major word stress' over roots and inflected words; no phrasal/clausal prominence domain is invoked."
255.prule: No positional rule survives, either as an exceptionless or as a dominant pattern. Per word length, Merlan 1983:29-31 gives: 2sigma mostly 10, with listed final-stress exceptions (jurer?, galay, gunman?); 3sigma two co-equal major patterns 100 and 010; 4sigma at least three patterns (major-initial 1'23`4, its variant 1`23'4, and 12'34, major stress on the second syllable and no other major stress on the root); 5sigma mostly 00100 (antepenult), some 00010 (penult), reduplicative 01000; 6sigma mostly 000010 (penult), a few antepenult; inflected words are root-anchored, not word-edge-counted (bigur-yi? keeps root stress, defeating penult counting), with documented free variation (ŋu-wákena ~ ŋu-wakéna, bíṇ-gagaʔ ~ biṇ-gágaʔ, ŋu-ṛábon-jiʔ ~ ŋu-ṛabón-jiʔ). No single pattern per word length exists, so the language is not classed as fixed stress.
255.srule: Merlan 1983:30-31 states secondary stress only piecemeal: in quadrisyllabic roots 'sometimes a secondary stress on the alternate (third) syllable' when major stress is initial (bi'dipi`di, da'kbara`ra), or 'if detectible on the first syllable' when major stress is on the third (mi`liba'lkin~); bisyllabic nominal suffixes (-ka'ga?~-ga'ga?, -ga'pul, -pu'lu) and past-continuous -miyin bear at least secondary stress; nothing for other lengths. Baker 1999:35-36, 45-46 and Baker 2005:4-5 give the rule: regular trochaic alternation from the first syllable (ka'n.amu`ru, ka'r.angkangan.ini), no final stress; in quadrisyllables feet on syllables 1 and 3 with either head primary; polysyllabic suffixes and each compound member carry their own foot, the rightmost head primary and the others secondary.
255.quote: The description of stress given here is far from complete; mention only is made of some basic stress patterns in roots and words. There is a tendency for word-stress to be penultimate, but many kinds of factors can prevent this seeming tendency from being realised. One of these factors is that there are variable patterns of root stress, and another, that a number of bisyllabic nominal and verbal suffixes cannot take a major stress, so that stress must occur earlier in the inflected word. ... There are two major patterns in trisyllabic nominal and adverbial roots: 1́ 2 3 and 1 2́ 3.
255.idn: Ngalakan, as spoken at Bulman, Roper Valley Station and Ngukurr (Roper River region, Arnhem Land, Northern Territory); no dialect named; data: p. viii: 'My first inquiries about Ngalakan were made in 1976 during a brief trip to Bulman from Bamyili... In 1977, while living at Jembere Aboriginal community on the…
255.exq_: There is a tendency for word-stress to be penultimate, but many kinds of factors can prevent this seeming tendency from being realised. ... Most bisyllabic roots have penultimate stress ... though a handful of nouns (juṛérʔ friarbird), interjections (gaḷáy hey!, look out!) and other parts of speech…

(No statement of how stress was observed; patterns are reported as e.g. 'Five-syllable roots mostly showed the pattern ...', 'a handful of nouns ... were found to have final root stress'. morph.stmt: Ngalakan combines obligatory prefixation (noun-class prefixes on nominals; portmanteau subject/object pronominal prefixes plus c.20 'preverbal' number/aspect/modal/applicative prefixes on the verb) with suffixal case, number, possession, tense-aspect, negation and derivation: Merlan's verb template (p.93) is gu- + Pronominal Prefix(es) + Preverbal Prefixes + Compounding element + ROOT + AUX + RR + TNS/ASP + NEG + NUM + SUB, and the Introduction (p.v-vi) characterises the group as showing 'considerable development of nominal case-marking by suffixes', 'fairly complex verbal morphology of an agglutinative to mildly fusional sort, with factitives, causatives and other verbal derivations…

tn.quote: In all three languages, the main form of prosodic prominence is pitch accent, which is anchored to stressed syllables. … prominence is mostly limited to pitch, associated with phrasal accentuation. … All these languages allocate stress as a mostly predicable edge-based phenomenon of Σ and ω constituents … In Ngalakgan only, there is secondary and primary stress, realised as accentual upstep … In monomorphemic forms the prosodic head, indicated by H* accent anchoring, may be on the left-most foot (as in examples above), or at least for some words, may optionally be on the right-most foot

tn.note: No lexical tone: pitch is a phrasal H* accent anchored to stressed syllables (bimoraic trochaic feet, left- or right-headed words); secondary-to-primary stress shows as accentual upstep.

255.cfw: Merlan 1983 describes, in a stress section she calls 'far from complete', a tendency to penultimate stress with variable root stress, but Baker 1999 (revised as Baker 2008), a book-length study of Ngalakgan word structure repeated in Baker 2005, finds initial primary stress in simple words, medial stress only on heavy syllables, and initial-or-penultimate variation in four-syllable roots, so the two first-hand accounts genuinely differ on placement and type but the fuller study is the clear guide.

256.dq: Utterances are divided into stress groups or feet; stress will occur on the final syllable of a foot, unless that foot occurs before a pause, then stress will be on the penultimate of the foot. (Hyman 1977:42)
256.dloc: the StressTyp2 entry; Migliazza & Grimes 1961:35 (etnolinguistica.org scan in the copy consulted): "Every foot also has one loud stress. This occurs on the penult or ultima of the foot - on the penult of a foot that is at the end of a pause group, on the ultima of all other feet." define the foot as the third level of the phonological hierarchy "characterized by features of juncture and stress"; StressTyp2 word 2340 is a whole sentence of five feet
256.prule: Every foot (the stress group, third level of the source's hierarchy syllable < foot < contour < pause group; about one word each in the printed examples, though the source never names the word) has one loud stress: on the ultima of every foot except the last foot of a pause group, which is stressed on the penult ('Paroxytonic feet occur only at the end of pause groups; all other feet are oxytonic'); forms cited in isolation are given in their pause-group-final (penult) shape unless hyphened (Note 3). Stress is 'phonemically nondistinctive' and predictable from the foot boundaries and the foot's position in the pause group.
256.srule: Reduced (secondary) stress on the second syllable before the loud stress in feet of more than three syllables (one unstressed syllable in between; a single reduced stress, not iterated); if the second or third syllable before the loud stress is a bare V syllable preceded by another syllable, the reduced stress falls on the syllable before that V. Restated at word level by Migliazza 1972:162, A.P.2 ('secondary stress is placed on the second vowel preceding the primary stressed vowel').
256.quote: Every foot also has one loud stress. This occurs on the penault or ultima of the foot - on the penult of a foot that is at the end of a pause group, on the ultima of all other feet. Accordingly, the minimum foot that can occur at the end of a pause group is a two-syllable one, whereas the minimum foot that can occur elsewhere is a one-syllable one.

256.tone: none (pitch is intonational: contour pitch levels 1-4, 'prephonemic approximations', with normal and suspended terminals; stress 'phonemically nondistinctive', M&G 1961:36)

While nouns can occur in isolation as phonological words and pause groups, verbs cannot and have to take pronouns and suffixes." morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing/post-posing: Migliazza 1972 p.141 "When all these constituents are present the verb surface order is generally verb root, causative-reflexive, adverb(s), inchoative, aspect" (with modals and negatives following the aspect, p.109 "Aspect suffixes occur after adverbs, causative and inchoative morphemes. Only modals may follow them"), noun case, plural, comitative and possessive markers are suffixes or postposed enclitics/particles (p.154 "the few suffixes which appear on the surface usually as a consonant", -n agent, -k plural, e genitive), while the only pre-root material is the proclitic weak subject/object pronouns…

257.prule: Stress on the first syllable and on every alternate syllable after it ('Stress tends to occur on the first and every alternate syllable', p.65: ['palə'gi], ['mɨsi'wʌnəŋ]). The source writes all stresses with one mark and does not say which is primary.
257.srule: Every alternate syllable after the first is stressed (odd-numbered syllables from the left): 3-syll ['palə'gi], ['daba'bi]; 4-syll ['misi'wʌnəŋ], ['ligəl'tɛki]. The source uses one stress mark throughout and does not rank the stresses; no word of five or more syllables is transcribed, so 10101, 101010... rest on the wording of the rule.

morph.rootq: "Stress tends to occur on the first and every alternate syllable. ... There are a few two syllable words where the stress seems to be on the second syllable. /gʌr̃ɨg/ [gʌ'r̃ɨg] 'head', /pɨlɨg/ [pə'lɨg] 'cheek', /nɨpr̃i/ [nəp'r̃i] 'star', /nɨplay/ [nəp'lay] 'sky, cloud'. When there is a prefix added, stress may be on the second syllable. /pəwɛgʌr̃/ [pə'wɛgʌr̃] [pʰə'wɛⁱgʌr̃] 'tame' (possessive prefix 'pə')" (Manning & Saggers 1977:65, §5.1). [The rule itself is stated over the word; the only morphological reference is that a syllabic prefix may be skipped so that stress lands on the stem-initial syllable.]
morph.elicq: No method sentence is given. §0: "The following material was collected during the time 4th October 1974 to 16th November 1974, at Yabiru, near Ningil in the Western Sepik District of Papua New Guinea." §3: "We have recorded only those that we actually heard." The stress section (§5.1, p.65) rests entirely on impressionistic phonetic transcriptions of single citation words, e.g. "/paligi/ ['palə'gi] [pʰalə'gi] '(subject person) give me'", "/mɨsiwʌnɨŋ/ ['mɨsi'wʌnəŋ] 'woman'", "/lɨgɨltɛki/ ['lɨgəl'tɛⁱki] 'jaw, chin'"; the two-sentence sample text (p.71) carries stress marks but is not used in the stress statement. Coded isolated-words by inference from the presentation, not from an explicit…
morph.stmt: The only Ningil source is a phonology and makes no overall morphological statement; what its glossed word pairs show is a split profile: subject person on verbs is marked by word-initial consonant prefixes (g- 1sg, m- 1pl/3pl.m, w- 3sg.f, l- 3pl.f), there is a 'possessive prefix pə-' (p.65), while noun plural (and verbal object number, gilʌn/gilʌŋ) is marked at the right edge by suffixes or final-segment alternation. This matches Laycock's (1975:768, 770-771) Torricelli-phylum characterization: "Subject-concordance is indicated by a set of prefixes to verbs, which are remarkably consistent throughout the whole phylum" and nouns have "irregular morphological plurals, sometimes…
